His belt loops. Under the radio clip. Still nothing. It seemed Herman had pocketed his cuff keys while searching him. Fantastic. “Of course he did,” Leon muttered under his breath, voice dry. “Why wouldn’t he?” Glancing around the room didn’t offer anything much to help either. Trays stacked in one corner, two overturned gurneys, an IV pole across the floor like a tripping hazard that never got cleaned up. Lots of metal, but anything sharp or sturdy enough to pry with was too far away to test out. He reached out, more careful this time, fingers sweeping what debris was within arm’s length. A toppled tray. The edge of an overturned gurney. Something that might’ve once been a pen but was now too bent to be useful. Not even so much as a staple or paperclip to pick the lock with, not that he had ever been really good at it. That was more Jill's specialty from what the others had told him. "Looks like I'm waiting, then. Damnit. Just had to get the one guy who is willing to improvise." He leaned his head back against the metal, rubbing at his wrenched shoulder with his free hand, and closed his eyes. Just for a second. Just to think. Not like he was going anywhere. The cuff rattled sharply as Leon pulled against the chain, testing for any give. The cabinet creaked, but didn’t budge. “C’mon,” he growled under his breath, planting his boots and bracing into the motion. The metal groaned again, louder this time, but still held firm. Another tug. Another ache in his wrist. Still no movement. In the distance, he could pick up the sounds of the others moving quickly around the building. The Doctor's thudding steps were easy enough to pick up even without the weird aura field that set his heart hammering in his head, and the speed of the smaller scuffing steps told him that a chase was on nearby. Fast. Light. Meg, maybe? Not likely Jake either way. Good. With how annoyed the Doctor was at Jake right now, he might decide to get creative there too. Best to let him take out his frustration on some normal hook kills. Unpleasant, but at least everyone knew what to expect. Sharp stab, a brief moment of terror, then back to the campfire to rest. Not too terrible in the long run. He stilled for a moment, listening. The uneven echo of sprinting feet. The skittering scrape of something being vaulted. Then that familiar electric crackle in the air — a rising static hum that meant only one thing: Herman had eyes on them. The air shifted, sharp and metallic. Leon stiffened. He’d felt that before. The lead-up to one of the Doctor’s area-wide shocks — a burst meant to disorient, slow reaction times, force mistakes. Of course, he would be trying to slow the survivor down, scramble them just enough to confuse movement. It always stung, and everyone had long since learned the taste in the air that preceded it. The shock wave passed easily through the far wall, sparks dancing in white arcs from corner to corner. He followed the flickers with his eyes — arcs of energy crawling across desk legs, chair frames, handles. Everything metal. Metal. His eyes locked on the metal cuff. The realization hit him a breath too late. The shockwave hit the filing cabinet like lightning striking a weathervane. The pain was instant, blinding, slicing through the cuff and across his bones, discharging across flesh and muscle alike. Every nerve lit up like copper wire in a furnace. His scream tangled in his throat as his knees buckled, limbs locking against the intrusion in violent lurches. His hip slammed against the cabinet on the way back to the floor, and for one breathless second, he hung there — suspended by his arm, muscles locked, nerves screaming. He gasped sharply as the chase passed by, then choked on the tail end of it, body twitching as the last of the voltage bled out through him, leaving him gasping and grasping at the cement of the floor as if it could somehow anchor his nerves back in place. He didn’t remember falling. Only the pain. And the taste of metal in the back of his throat. His arm was stretched painfully above him, cuffed wrist still locked to the cabinet. His body had collapsed at an angle — one hip on the floor, the other twisted awkwardly against the base of the unit. His legs shook beneath him, muscles twitching from the aftershock. The room smelled like burnt ozone now. Like the air just after a lightning strike. Leon stayed down for a while, breathing through clenched teeth, trying to will his nerves into compliance. Eventually, the tremors softened enough to let him sit up straighter. Leon pressed his back to the cabinet, breath hitching as he tried to ease the strain from his arm. The muscles in his shoulder burned from the jolt. Every nerve felt skinned raw, still catching echoes of the voltage that had torn through him. His fingers were numb. The cuff bit deep into raw skin. He took another look around the room, a horrified understanding slowly coming to the surface. It wasn’t just cluttered. It was loaded . Metal trays. Surgical carts. Gurneys with chrome legs. Even the cabinet he was chained to had rivets and handles begging to carry current. Every piece of furniture in here had a conductive surface. The static had nowhere else to go but through the one organic thing grounded in the room. And this room? It was in the middle of everything . He knew this layout well.
